alerts.details: 3 failed sign-ins for {user}, then a successful one. Same laptop and office network ({lan}) {user} has used every day this month.
alerts.why: A typo pattern from a known device and network. Note it and close.
alerts.next: Close as benign. If it keeps happening, suggest a password manager.

alerts.details: The firewall blocked {n} connection attempts from {ip} across 20 ports in 2 minutes. No connection was allowed through.
alerts.why: Internet background noise that the firewall already stopped. Nothing got in.
alerts.next: Close. Check the address's reputation and confirm the block rule is in place.

alerts.details: Antivirus quarantined a file in {user}'s Downloads folder on {host} before it ever ran. No other alerts on {host} in the last 24 hours.
alerts.why: The control worked: the file was caught before it ran and nothing else looks wrong.
alerts.next: Close after confirming the quarantine succeeded, and remind {user} about downloads.

alerts.details: {user} signed in to {host} as an administrator at 23:40 from {lan}. Change ticket CHG-{n4} schedules maintenance on {host} at 23:30 tonight, owned by {user}.
alerts.why: Unusual hour, but it matches an approved change owned by the same person.
alerts.next: Close and link the alert to CHG-{n4} so the next analyst sees why.

alerts.details: {host} uploaded 40 GB to the company's approved backup service at 02:00. It has done the same every night for a year.
alerts.why: Big, but expected: a known destination on a long-standing schedule.
alerts.next: Close, and consider tuning the rule to skip the backup job.

alerts.details: Internal scanner {lan} probed every server in the {host} subnet. The security team's weekly scan is scheduled for today.
alerts.why: It's our own scheduled scanner doing its job.
alerts.next: Close and add the scanner to the rule's allowlist.

alerts.details: {user} signed in from two countries 10 minutes apart. An MFA prompt was approved for the second sign-in.
alerts.why: Nobody travels that fast, and the approved MFA prompt suggests the person was tricked into approving it.
alerts.next: Escalate: revoke {user}'s sessions, reset the password and review what the account accessed.

alerts.details: A Word document {user} opened on {host} started PowerShell with an encoded command. The file arrived by email from an outside sender.
alerts.why: Word almost never needs to launch scripts. This is a common first step of an email-borne infection.
alerts.next: Escalate: isolate {host}, keep the document as evidence and check who else received the email.

alerts.details: {host} has contacted {ip} every 60 seconds for 6 hours. The domain behind it was registered yesterday.
alerts.why: Clockwork connections to a brand-new domain look like malware checking in for instructions.
alerts.next: Escalate: isolate {host}, block the domain and search for other machines talking to it.

alerts.details: A new rule in {user}'s mailbox forwards every incoming email to an outside address. {user} says they didn't create it.
alerts.why: Hidden forwarding rules are a classic sign of a taken-over mailbox quietly leaking mail.
alerts.next: Escalate: remove the rule, secure {user}'s account and work out what was forwarded.

alerts.details: Files on the shared drive on {host} are being renamed with a new extension at hundreds per minute, and a text file with the same name appeared in every folder.
alerts.why: This is what ransomware looks like while it's running. Minutes matter.
alerts.next: Escalate immediately: isolate {host} and the account doing the renames, and start the incident response plan.

alerts.details: Endpoint protection on {host} was switched off by a local account. No change ticket, and {user}, who uses {host}, isn't an administrator.
alerts.why: Attackers often turn off security tools first. Unexplained and unapproved is enough to escalate.
alerts.next: Escalate: turn protection back on, isolate {host} and find out which account did it.
